title: Cannot bound a hung provider call: a timed deref does not preempt a blocking FFI read
description:
A provider call that hangs cannot be bounded from inside the process, and it takes the whole beam with it.

The scheduler gives each branch turn a hard deadline and derefs the future with a timeout, on the assumption that a blown deadline forfeits only that branch's turn. That assumption is false when the thread is parked in a blocking FFI call: a timed `deref` does not preempt it. The branch stays parked, and because the scheduler is a barrier per turn, every other branch waits behind it.

Observed twice. A Phase 4 beam froze for fifteen minutes with three branches idle behind one. The full benchmark sweep died on it: one run sat for thirty-one minutes against a 420-second deadline, inside a socket read that never returned. `:socket-timeout` on the clj-http-lite request did not fire either.

This is the one open problem that limits what the harness can do. Everything else has a workaround.

Options, none of them a patch:

- Run the provider call in a subprocess that can be killed. Expensive per call, but the kill is unconditional and matches the RAX-manager principle the rest of the loop already follows: the stop path must not depend on the component's cooperation.
- A watchdog thread that closes the socket underneath the parked reader, which turns the block into an I/O error the existing catch handles. Needs a socket handle the client does not currently expose.
- Give up on bounding it and make the scheduler pipeline rather than barrier, so a parked branch costs only itself. Cheaper to build and does not fix the parked thread, which accumulates.

Until one of these lands, concurrency above roughly six in-flight provider calls should be treated as unsafe, and the benchmark sweep runs at `:concurrency 2`.
design:
## Ruled out: buffering journal writes

An in-memory queue drained into SQLite by a writer thread was considered and
does not address this. The stall is a branch thread parked in recv() inside
jolt.http-client; it never reaches a write. Confirmed in the code: llm/chat sits
outside any with-conn, and record-turn! only runs after it returns, so no DB
lock is ever held across a provider call.

That design is still worth doing for its own reasons and is filed as veriframe-clj-dpj.
It is recorded here so nobody re-proposes it against this issue.

## Chosen mitigation: stop joining every branch each round

advance-all derefs every branch's future before the round ends. That barrier is
what turns one parked branch into a stalled beam. If the scheduler instead
collected whatever COMPLETED and carried the rest forward as still-in-flight, a
hung branch would cost only itself.

This does not remove the parked thread, which still leaks a socket and a Chez
thread for the life of the process. It downgrades the failure from "the run
dies" to "one branch is lost and the beam continues", which is most of the
practical value and is what makes the benchmark sweep completable.

The work is in the three places that currently assume they see every branch's
post-turn state:

- culling reads consecutive-failures, which an in-flight branch has not updated
- forking reads pending-branch-theses off a settled branch
- the done check scans for a final answer

Each needs to tolerate "this branch has not reported yet" rather than treating
absence as a state. The branch-count arithmetic in the cull rule also has to
count in-flight branches as alive, or a beam with one slow branch and one
failing branch would cull the failing one on the grounds that nobody else is
running.

## Still open after the mitigation

Bounding the call itself. Two options, neither a patch:

- Run the provider call in a subprocess that can be killed. Unconditional, and
  matches the RAX-manager principle the rest of the loop follows: the stop path
  must not depend on the component's cooperation. Costs a process per call.
- A watchdog that closes the socket underneath the parked reader, turning the
  block into an I/O error the existing catch already handles. Cheaper, but needs
  a socket handle jolt.http-client does not currently expose, so it likely means
  a change upstream or a fork of the client.

Until one lands, keep concurrent provider calls under about six and run the
benchmark sweep at :concurrency 2.
close_reason:
Fixed upstream in jolt-lang/http-client cc45d7e. Root cause was not that a blocking FFI read is unbounded in principle, but that connect-stream took a read-timeout and applied it only on the plaintext branch — tls-connect opened its socket without SO_RCVTIMEO, so :socket-timeout had no effect on any https request and every provider call is https. Now applied. Against a TLS server that completes the handshake and then never answers, a 2000ms socket-timeout gives up at 2074ms with a SocketTimeoutException; before the fix the same request ran past 45 minutes. Regression test: jolt.http.timeout-test/https-honours-socket-timeout, under the :timeouttest alias.

The scheduler mitigation this bead designed (pipeline instead of barrier) is NOT needed and was not implemented — the barrier was only fatal because one branch could park forever, which it no longer can.

Two residuals, both deliberately left: :conn-timeout is still ignored, because setting O_NONBLOCK needs variadic fcntl and Apple arm64 passes variadic args on the stack, so a fixed-arity binding silently corrupts them (F_SETFL with 6 read back as 194, O_NONBLOCK unset) — connect is at least kernel-bounded by the SYN retry limit, unlike recv. And SO_RCVTIMEO bounds inactivity rather than total duration, filed separately.

title: Every jolt-lang dependency is unlicensed, which blocks distributing this under GPLv3
description:
Every dependency this project has declares no licence. Checked via the GitHub API on 2026-08-05:

    jolt-lang/jolt                NONE
    jolt-lang/http-client         NONE
    jolt-lang/db                  NONE
    jolt-lang/jolt-crypto         NONE
    jolt-lang/nrepl               NONE
    jolt-lang/time                NONE
    jolt-lang/logging             NONE
    jolt-lang/ring-chez-adapter   NONE

No LICENSE file in any repository and no SPDX id reported. Without an explicit grant the default under copyright is all rights reserved, which means there is no stated permission to redistribute them, and none to link them into a GPLv3 work.

This matters more now than it did yesterday, for two reasons. The project relicensed to GPLv3, which is a licence whose whole mechanism is conditions on distribution, so shipping it while its entire dependency graph is unlicensed is incoherent. And vendor/ring_chez/adapter.clj is not merely depended on but COPIED INTO THIS REPOSITORY, so the ambiguity is distributed with the source rather than resolved at build time by a user who fetches it themselves. That file now carries a note saying so, and is the only source file without a veriframe copyright header.

Nothing here is an accusation. These are all repositories under the same umbrella as the language itself and the intent is obviously that people use them; the licences are simply missing. The fix is to ask upstream to add one. MIT or Apache-2.0 on the libraries would be ideal, since both are GPLv3-compatible in the direction needed and neither constrains other consumers.

Concretely:

- Open an issue on each jolt-lang repository asking for an explicit licence. One issue on jolt-lang/jolt covering all of them is probably the better opening move.
- ring-chez-adapter is the urgent one because its code is vendored here. If upstream will not licence it, the options are to rewrite the adapter from scratch, or to drop the vendored copy and take the upstream dependency so the copy is not redistributed. Note the local change is small and documented, so a clean reimplementation is not a large job.
- Until this resolves, do not cut a tagged release or publish a binary. Running it locally and developing against it is unaffected.

Filed rather than fixed because it is not this project's code to relicence, and the resolution is a conversation with upstream rather than a commit here.
close_reason:
Resolved, and the resolution reversed the licence decision that prompted it.

Two corrections to what this bead claimed. It said all eight jolt-lang repositories were unlicensed; two were not, and my check was wrong (`gh repo view --json licenseInfo` reported NONE across the board, while the REST `.license.spdx_id` gives the real answer). jolt was already EPL-2.0 and logging EPL-1.0. It also implied this needed an upstream conversation; there is admin access on every one of those repositories, so it did not.

Six libraries genuinely had no licence and now have EPL-2.0, matching jolt and Clojure convention: http-client, db, jolt-crypto, nrepl, time, ring-chez-adapter. All eight now report a licence.

`clj-commons/clj-http-lite` also reported as unlicensed and is not. It is MIT, declared in its pom.xml and its README, with no LICENSE file for GitHub's detector to find. Nothing to do, and the claim in this bead was wrong.

The larger finding was that GPLv3 was never viable. jolt is EPL-2.0 with the secondary-licence option NOT exercised (its Exhibit A is the unfilled template, and the licence text says including Exhibit A alone is not sufficient), and data.json, tools.logging and jolt-lang/logging are EPL-1.0 by inheritance from Clojure code that is not ours to relicense. The FSF lists EPL as GPL-incompatible in both versions. So a GPLv3 veriframe could not legally link its own platform, whatever happened to the unlicensed libraries.

veriframe is EPL-2.0 as of this change: LICENSE replaced, 51 file headers converted, README rewritten with the reasoning. The only thing that had required GPLv3 was embedding Octave in-process, and Octave moves to a subprocess like z3 and swipl, where its GPL does not reach across the process boundary. veriframe-clj-15u carries that change.

Every dependency is now compatible with EPL-2.0: EPL-2.0 for the jolt-lang libraries, EPL-1.0 for the Clojure-derived ones, MIT for clj-http-lite.

title: Mathlib import exceeds its timeout, so verify_lean and proof_start always fail
description:
The Lean engine is reachable as of veriframe-clj-iud and does not work. The first Lean tool call in a branch triggers mathlib-env, which sends `import Mathlib` and waits :timeout-ms, defaulting to 300000. Measured on this machine with warm oleans and no contention: the import takes 377927ms and then succeeds, and a subsequent theorem elaborates fine. So it is not hung. It is 26 percent over a ceiling that is simply too low, and every verify_lean / proof_start / proof_step call dies with "Could not import Mathlib: The Lean REPL did not reply within 300000ms and has been killed."

Raising the number is not the whole fix. :engines :lean :timeout-ms is used for BOTH the one-time import and every subsequent command, and those want opposite values: the import is a ~6.3 minute one-off, while a tactic that has not answered in six minutes is wedged and should be killed quickly. One knob cannot serve both, so this wants a separate import timeout with the per-command timeout left short.

Two related problems the measurement exposes.

The turn deadline is 420000ms (beam/default-turn-deadline-ms). A 377927ms import inside a single turn consumes 90 percent of it before the model does any work, so even with the timeout raised the first Lean turn is nearly guaranteed to blow the deadline.

Every branch builds its own Lean session, so a beam pays the import per branch. At the default beam width of 5 that is five separate six-minute imports competing for one machine. Importing once and sharing a read-only Mathlib environment across branches is the structural fix.

## Why this was invisible

Nothing could call the engine, so nothing ever measured it, and the assurances that existed were weaker than they looked. /health reports lean:true from a file-exists check. smoke/lean-check is (.exists (java.io.File. repl-bin)) -- it never starts the REPL and never imports anything, so "pass lean repl" meant only that a file was on disk. The CI lean job is the one real check and it does not gate pull requests. Neither smoke nor /health should report a green Lean engine on the strength of a file existing.
notes:
Second correction, and it identifies the cause. The import measures 23240ms on an idle machine. Every earlier six-minute figure was taken while 28 orphaned z3 processes (veriframe-clj-qm7) were consuming memory on a 16GB box already in swap, so Lean's mmapped oleans re-faulted every time.

The fixes still stand and are still worth having: the import and per-command timeouts genuinely differ, warming still moves the cost out of a branch turn, and a loaded or smaller machine will still see the slow behaviour. What is now clearly wrong is the sizing advice about one warm session per branch, which rested on a second import never being cheaper, and that was an artifact of the leak.
close_reason:
Fixed on three fronts, all measured rather than estimated.

**The timeout was one knob doing two jobs.** `:engines :lean :timeout-ms` covered both `import Mathlib` and every subsequent command, and those want opposite values. Split into `:timeout-ms` (per command, 300000) and `:import-timeout-ms` (1200000), with `send-command` taking a per-call override so only the import gets the generous ceiling. `HARNESS_LEAN_IMPORT_TIMEOUT_MS` exposes it.

**Warming moved the import out of the turn.** veriframe.engine.lean-pool warms sessions at startup on background threads, so `system/start!` returns immediately and the server answers /health while the import runs. A branch checks out a warmed session; if one is still importing it waits on that rather than starting a second beside it, and if the pool is empty or a warm failed it builds its own, so this is never a dependency. `system/stop!` disposes them.

**Other timeouts raised.** z3 and swipl 30000 to 120000, turn deadline 420000 to 900000. The deadline is now sized to the worst LEGITIMATE turn — a provider call at its 300000ms socket timeout plus a Lean tactic at its own — because forfeiting a turn that was about to succeed costs the branch the turn AND logs a failure other branches then avoid retrying.

## Measurements

Import cost, idle machine, warm olean cache: 377927ms, then 384334ms and 375026ms on a repeat run. Warmed at startup in the running harness: 354490ms.

A second import in the same process is NOT cheaper (384334 then 375026, a 2.4% difference that is noise). So the cost is CPU-bound elaboration, not disk, and the OS page cache does not help. That matters for sizing: one warm session helps exactly one branch, and a beam that genuinely uses Lean wants `HARNESS_LEAN_WARM_SESSIONS` equal to its width. A warmed session measures 0.83GB RSS, so 5 is about 4.2GB — the default stays 1 because most problems never touch Lean.

## Verified end to end

Booted with warming on: /health reported `{installed: true, warm_sessions: 0, warming: 1}` within 30 seconds, then `warm_sessions: 1` after 354516ms. A Lean problem then confirmed `verify_lean` ON TURN 1, and warm_sessions dropped 1 to 0 showing the checkout. Three confirmed Lean artifacts in the run. Before this change the first Lean call always died at the 300000ms import timeout.

## Also fixed here

The false assurances this bead named. /health now reports `lean.warm_sessions` and `lean.warming` next to `engines.lean`, because installed and ready are different things and conflating them is how the health check stayed green while every Lean call failed. smoke/lean-check was `(.exists (File. repl-bin))`; it now actually imports Mathlib and elaborates a theorem, which makes the probe slow and able to fail the way the engine fails.

Suite 63 tests / 356 assertions green, including veriframe.pool-test covering the checkout bookkeeping offline — no session issued twice under concurrency, a still-importing slot returned to the pool rather than leaked, a failed warm falling through to nil.

Still open and filed separately: sharing one Mathlib environment across branches instead of one session each, which is the structural fix the per-branch cost argues for.

title: The six Lean tools are absent from the system prompt, so the Lean engine is unreachable
description:
resources/prompts/system.md documents 11 tools. veriframe.agent.tools/run-tool dispatches 17. The six missing are all of Lean: verify_lean, lean_search, proof_start, proof_step, proof_state, proof_abandon.

A model cannot call a tool it was never told exists, so the entire Lean path is dead in practice: the long-lived leanprover-community/repl session, the grep-backed Mathlib premise index with its synonym map, tools/setup-lean.sh, and the CI lean job all exist and work, and nothing can reach them. /health reports lean:true, which makes it look available.

The cause is that the two are unconnected. loop/system-prompt is (slurp (io/resource "prompts/system.md")) — a hand-maintained file with no link to the dispatch table. Adding a defmethod does not add it to the prompt.

The irony is that agent_test/tool-table-is-complete exists precisely because a stray paren once hid 7 of 10 methods, and it pins the registry set at 17 while saying nothing about whether the prompt mentions them. tools/tool-names already exists and is used only by that test.

Fix has two parts. Document the six tools in system.md, which is the part that makes Lean usable. Then make the drift impossible: assert every name in (tools/tool-names) appears in the prompt text, so a new defmethod without a prompt entry fails the suite instead of silently never being called.

Worth re-checking the benchmark afterwards. Lean problems could not have been attempted, so any conclusion about theorem-proving performance was measuring an unreachable engine.
close_reason:
Fixed. All 17 dispatched tools are now documented in resources/prompts/system.md, organized by engine, plus a 'Choosing an engine' section so the model picks by problem shape rather than reading a flat menu, and a note on which tools reach the slow tier (verify_template, or a Lean proof closed with proof_step) — which the tier-escalation gate had been pushing branches toward without ever saying how to get there.

Also fixed the quieter instance of the same bug: verify_template's four templates were only listed in the error returned after guessing a wrong name, so a template the model never guessed was invisible. loop/system-prompt now substitutes the catalogue from smt-templates/list-templates, since it is pure data.

Drift is now guarded in both directions by veriframe.prompt-test: every name in tools/tool-names must appear in the prompt, and the prompt must name nothing run-tool cannot dispatch. Both were verified against a deliberately broken prompt rather than assumed — deleting proof_state and adding a fictional verify_coq each fail with the right message. Suite is 56 tests / 339 assertions green.

Verified live: on a non-finite problem (sum of first n odds = n^2), both branches reached for Lean unprompted — B1 called verify_lean, B2 called lean_search, which returned real Mathlib hits. Neither tool was reachable before.

That run also exposed a defect this bead was hiding: verify_lean fails because the Mathlib import exceeds its timeout. Filed separately — it was invisible for as long as nothing could invoke the engine.

title: Orphaned z3 processes accumulate and are never reaped
description:
28 orphaned `z3` processes were found on the dev machine, the oldest running 17 hours 43 minutes, holding roughly 450MB each at the top end. They survive the harness that spawned them and are never reaped.

Found incidentally while measuring Mathlib import cost: they were competing for CPU and contaminating the measurement, which is a second reason to care. A benchmark sweep that leaves dozens of z3 processes behind is also slowly poisoning its own timings.

engine/proc.clj `run` calls `p/destroy-tree` on timeout, so the timeout path looks right. Candidates for where they escape:

- A branch turn abandoned at the deadline. The scheduler stops waiting, but the work keeps running and whatever it spawned is never destroyed, because the deadline fires in the scheduler and the `finally` that would reap lives in the abandoned thread. This is the same shape as the Lean session problem that send-command's kill-on-busy already addresses, and z3 has no equivalent.
- Run abort. `control/abort` stops scheduling; nothing walks the branches disposing engine subprocesses.
- Process exit without the shutdown hook running, e.g. SIGKILL during development.

Worth checking whether swipl leaks the same way; only z3 was counted here because swipl sessions are long-lived and per-branch, so they are more visible.

Fix likely wants engine subprocesses tracked per branch and disposed when the branch ends for any reason, including abort and deadline forfeit, rather than relying on each call site's `finally`. veriframe.engine.lean-pool/shutdown! is the shape to copy: system/stop! disposes warmed Lean sessions and those were reaped correctly in the same session that leaked 28 z3s.

Not urgent for correctness — a leaked z3 has already returned its answer and affects nothing but memory and CPU contention. It is a resource and measurement-hygiene problem, and it makes long benchmark runs progressively slower and less trustworthy.
notes:
This leak was the cause of the Mathlib slowness that drove the whole warming investigation, which makes it more than a hygiene problem.

Measurements of 'import Mathlib' on this machine, in order:

    377927ms   with 28 orphaned z3 processes running
    384334ms   same
    375026ms   same
    354490ms   same
     23240ms   after killing them

A 16x difference. The orphans were holding up to 450MB each on a 16GB machine that was already 2.3GB into swap, so Lean's ~7GB of mmapped oleans re-faulted from disk on every import. That is also why a second import in the same process looked no cheaper: the working set could not stay resident.

So the honest cost of importing Mathlib here is about 23 seconds, and the six-minute figure was this bug wearing a costume. veriframe-clj-j3j carries the correction.

The knock-on effects are worth stating because they show the blast radius: a false premise about Lean's cost, an over-generous import timeout, sizing advice about warm sessions per branch that does not hold, and every benchmark timing taken during that period being suspect.
close_reason:
Fixed, and the cause was not in this project's process handling. It was that no engine call was ever bounded at all.

jolt's clojure.core/deref invokes a record's `deref` method with only the value itself and drops any opts, so the timed three-arity (deref ref timeout-ms timeout-value) silently becomes the blocking one-arity for a record implementing IBlockingDeref. babashka.process implements it exactly that way. Measured directly: (deref proc 2000 ::timeout) on a `sleep 60` waited the full sixty seconds and returned the real result rather than ::timeout.

So proc/run never saw ::timeout, destroy-tree never ran, and the timeout branch was unreachable code. The orphans were branches abandoned at their deadline while proc/run was still blocked, leaving the subprocess with nobody to reap it. Every hypothesis in the original description was aimed at the reaping and none of them was it.

It fails in the quietest possible direction: no error, no warning, and the returned value is the correct result of a call that merely took longer than the caller allowed.

proc/run now waits with .waitFor and an explicit timeout, which the host implements correctly (it polls at 10ms and returns false). Reaping escalates SIGTERM to SIGKILL rather than stopping at destroy-tree, which sends only SIGTERM, on the grounds the rest of this loop already applies: a process being killed for ignoring its deadline is exactly the one that may ignore a polite signal.

Verified. Three 2000ms timeouts against `sleep 60` return in about 2.8s each with nothing left behind. A live two-branch run exercising verify_smt and verify_template completed with z3, swipl and repl counts all zero afterwards. Regression tests in engine-test, checked against the old implementation rather than assumed.

Upstream fix opened as jolt-lang/jolt#537 with make unit passing and make cts matching baseline. Nothing here waits on it.

Worth recording what this cost while it was unfixed, because it was more than wasted CPU. The accumulated orphans held up to 450MB each on a 16GB machine already in swap, which made Lean's mmapped oleans re-fault on every import and put `import Mathlib` at ~377s instead of ~23s. That drove an entire investigation into Lean startup cost, a warm-session pool, an import timeout sized to the wrong number, and sizing advice about warm sessions per branch that does not hold. See the corrections on veriframe-clj-j3j. Any benchmark timing taken before this fix should be treated as suspect.

title: Bind Z3's C API in-process instead of shelling out
description:
Bind Z3's C API through jolt.ffi and hold a live solver per branch, replacing
the current shell-out to the `z3` binary.

## Why this is an easier case than Octave (veriframe-clj-15u)

Z3 ships `z3_api.h` and exports 789 unmangled `Z3_*` symbols. jolt.ffi can bind
them directly — no `extern "C"` shim, no C++ toolchain, no build step. The C API
is the officially supported one; Z3's C++ API is a header-only wrapper over it,
so binding C is not a workaround but the intended path.

Z3 is MIT, so there is no licensing consequence either way. The GPLv3 move was
for Octave alone.

Everything needed is present: Z3_mk_context, Z3_eval_smtlib2_string,
Z3_solver_check, Z3_solver_push, Z3_solver_pop, Z3_model_get_const_interp,
Z3_get_numeral_string, Z3_set_error_handler.

## What it buys

**parse-model goes away.** engine/smt.clj currently walks Z3's printed
`(get-model)` output paren-balanced by hand, because printed text is all a
subprocess returns. It is the most fragile code in the engines and it has already
needed a special case for negatives printed as `(- 5)`. With the C API,
Z3_model_get_const_interp plus Z3_get_numeral_string returns values structurally,
and sorts come back as sorts rather than as strings to be guessed at.

**Error detection stops being text scraping.** The harness currently refuses a
verdict when it finds `(error ...)` lines in stdout, with a hand-maintained
whitelist for the benign "model is not available" case. With an installed error
handler, a parse or type error is reported as an error rather than inferred from
output, and the whitelist stops being load-bearing.

**Real incremental solving.** Z3_solver_push and Z3_solver_pop give what PLAN.md
originally sketched and the shell-out cannot do: a branch builds constraints
across turns, checks, and pops a bad hypothesis, the way the Prolog session
already lets it assert and retract. Today every verify_smt call re-submits the
whole formula from scratch, so the model pays to restate its encoding on every
turn and the harness cannot tell an added constraint from a rewritten one.

That last one is a capability gain rather than a cleanup, and is the strongest
argument here.

## The trade, which is real

The current subprocess is a crash boundary. A malformed input costs one call and
a non-zero exit; the harness reads the output and moves on. In-process, a Z3
crash takes the run and every other branch in the beam with it.

That matters more here than it would elsewhere, because the input is
model-generated and adversarial by nature — the SMT linter exists precisely
because models emit encodings that are wrong in surprising ways. Z3's default
error handler can abort the process outright, so Z3_set_error_handler is not
optional polish; without it a bad formula is a run-ending event.

Reference counting is the other hazard. Z3 objects are refcounted with
Z3_inc_ref/Z3_dec_ref and contexts must be freed. Getting that wrong through FFI
is a leak or a segfault, and this project has already produced one "invalid
memory reference" from FFI misuse (concurrent sqlite3_prepare_v2 on one handle).
A leak per verify_smt call across a long beam is not hypothetical.

So: worth doing, but the error handler and the refcount discipline are the work,
not the bindings.

## Keep the subprocess path

Do not delete it. Retain shell-out behind a config flag as the isolation-preserving
option, and because it is the only thing that will distinguish "Z3 disagrees" from
"our FFI binding is wrong" when a verdict looks suspicious. The two paths
answering differently on the same formula is a bug in the binding, and that is a
test worth having.

## Integration points

- `engine/z3_ffi.clj` — bindings, context and solver lifecycle, error handler
- `engine/smt.clj` — dispatch on the config flag; run-smt and run-template keep
  their current return shape so nothing above them changes
- a marshalling layer for models, replacing parse-model
- `:z3 {:mode :ffi | :subprocess}` in config.clj, subprocess remaining the default
  until the FFI path has run a full benchmark sweep without a crash
- solver handle on the branch, disposed by the scheduler like the Prolog session,
  with the same busy-flag guard against an abandoned turn

## Acceptance

- both paths return identical verdicts and identical witnesses across the whole
  benchmark registry; a disagreement is a binding bug and fails the suite
- a deliberately malformed formula is reported as an error and the process
  survives, mutation-tested by removing the error handler and watching it die
- no growth in resident memory across a thousand verify_smt calls
- push/pop exposed as a tool only after the above holds, since incremental state
  is the part that can silently corrupt a later verdict

title: Buffer journal appends through an atom, drained by one writer thread
description:
Journal appends should go through an in-memory queue drained by a single writer
thread, rather than each branch writing under a global lock.

The current store serializes ALL access to the connection, reads included,
because every read also calls sqlite3_prepare_v2 on the same handle and
concurrent prepares crash. That was the right emergency fix (it turned a sweep
that failed all fourteen problems into one that ran), but it is heavier than
necessary: context-block's failure-log query runs on every branch turn and now
contends with every other branch's appends.

With one writer thread there is exactly one thread preparing writes, so the lock
comes off the branch threads entirely and reads only contend with the drainer.

## What can be queued, and what cannot

The enabler is that the loop never reads its own state back from the DB. It
works from in-memory branch state, so a deferred append is not something anything
is waiting on.

Queue these. High volume, nothing reads them back synchronously:

- turns
- artifacts
- failures, with its failures_fts row kept adjacent in the same batch so the
  rowid pairing stays correct
- events

Keep these synchronous. Low volume, and each returns something a caller needs
immediately:

- runs and branches lifecycle
- gate_firings, because record-gate! returns the row id and the loop holds it to
  settle the prediction later. Defer this and there is no id to hold.
- interventions, because submit! returns an id to the HTTP caller.

## Three things the drainer has to get right

**It must fail loudly.** If the writer thread throws, the queue grows forever and
the journal silently stops while the run looks healthy. That is the same shape as
the progress-stalled gate that referenced a missing prompt file and had never
once worked: a mechanism that fails silently is indistinguishable from one that
is quiet. The thread's death has to surface.

**flush! has to block until drained**, and be called at run end, on abort, and by
the journal-tail endpoint before it serves. The last of those gives the API
read-your-writes without the loop having to know about it.

**It trades against a stated design goal.** "Append as it happens" is why a
crashed run stays inspectable, and a queue drained at intervals loses up to one
interval. At ~200ms against 30-second turns that is a fraction of a turn, and
flush! covers the orderly exits, but a hard kill loses the tail. Write that into
the docstring rather than leaving it to be discovered.

The failure-log staleness this introduces is one interval against 30-second
turns, so cross-branch sharing is unaffected in practice.

## Acceptance

- with-conn drops back to writes-only, since the drainer is the sole writer
- the existing store tests pass unchanged
- a test asserts that a drainer that throws surfaces rather than silently
  queueing, exercised by breaking it deliberately
- a test asserts flush! actually blocks until the queue is empty
- the benchmark sweep runs at a concurrency that previously crashed the store
close_reason:
Not building it. Measured first, and the contention this was written to remove is about 0.027% of a branch turn.

## Measurements

Against the real store, EPL-2.0 tree, 2026-08-05:

    journal write, single thread      median 2.49ms   max 11.2ms
    FTS read, uncontended             median 0.23ms   max  0.53ms
    FTS read, 5 concurrent writers    median 2.45ms   max  6.9ms
    FTS read, 12 concurrent writers   median 0.74ms   max 18.6ms

12 writers is the shape this bead cites (4 problems x 3 branches in the sweep). The read slowdown under contention is real and it is also sub-millisecond to low-millisecond.

From an actual completed Lean run: 25 turns produced 89 rows in total across turns, events, artifacts and failures, so about 3.6 writes per turn, and the average wall-clock gap between consecutive turns was 37453ms. That puts DB work at roughly 10ms in a 37-second turn, because the turn is dominated by a provider call and an engine call. Over a full run at beam width 5 and 80 turns the store accounts for a few seconds out of hours.

## Why the trade is bad, not merely unnecessary

The saving is unobservable. The costs are not:

Durability. Buffered rows are lost on a hard kill. That contradicts the property this system leads with -- everything appended as it happens so a crashed or aborted run stays fully inspectable -- and it is the property that lets a UI be a client rather than a special case. Trading it for 10ms is trading the thing for a rounding error on the thing it costs.

A silent failure mode. If the drainer thread dies the journal stops while the run looks healthy. This bead names that risk itself and compares it to the progress-stalled gate that referenced a missing prompt file and had never once worked. Adding a second mechanism with that shape, to save nothing measurable, is not a good exchange.

Coordination. flush! at run end, on abort, and in the journal-tail endpoint before it serves, each a place to get it wrong.

## The cheap alternative, also declined

WAL with synchronous=NORMAL was measured: write median 2.49ms to 1.73ms, but the tail worsens from 11ms to 53ms as checkpoints land, and reads under 12 writers were unchanged at ~0.7ms. WAL's real benefit is readers running concurrently with a writer, which the single conn-lock forecloses anyway. Not worth the change on these numbers; revisit if the lock ever comes off.

## When to reopen

If the store shows up in a profile. Concretely: if DB time exceeds a few percent of turn time, or if turn duration drops toward the tens of milliseconds where 10ms would matter. Neither is plausible while a provider call is in the loop.

The one thing that WOULD change this is dropping the global lock, since the lock is what makes reads wait behind writes at all. That is its own piece of work and would need the concurrent-prepare crash solved another way -- a second read-only connection is the obvious route, and it does not need a queue.

title: An AOT binary cannot complete a TLS handshake
description:
A binary from `jolt build` cannot complete a TLS handshake. Plain http works; https throws the same opaque Chez condition as veriframe-clj-9pl, but from the first call, with no nREPL involved.

Confirmed by driving the running binary over nREPL:

    :http  200
    :https THREW #object[:object]

The likely cause is that the OpenSSL natives declared under `:jolt/native` are not loaded into the image the way they are into an interpreted run, but that is a guess and has not been verified.

Consequences for this project:

- The binary is usable for the engine paths and against a local plain-http provider (llama-server, Ollama). It cannot talk to a hosted provider.
- It is why nREPL not starting in a binary costs nothing: a binary that cannot reach a provider is not the thing you attach an editor to.
- The `build` CI job therefore only asserts that the binary starts and serves `/health`, not that it can run the loop.

Also worth recording alongside this: `jolt build` embeds only what it can reach STATICALLY. A `requiring-resolve` in `system/start!` left the whole server and engine subtree out of the image, which then failed at startup trying to compile namespaces off source roots that do not exist. That part is fixed here by passing the handler var in from `core`, and the CI build job exists to catch a regression.
close_reason:
Fixed upstream in jolt-lang/http-client cc45d7e, same root cause as veriframe-clj-9pl. The guess recorded here was right: the OpenSSL declared under :jolt/native was not reaching the built image, so nothing loaded it and the SSL_* symbols fell through to the LibreSSL the macOS process image links. Not a distinct AOT problem — the same symbol-resolution hazard reached by a different route, which is why one fix closed both.

jolt.http.tls now loads libcrypto and libssl itself at ns init, which runs in a built image too.

Verified end to end on a jolt build binary: it completes a TLS handshake, validates the provider at boot ('provider :deepseek reachable, deepseek-v4-flash available'), starts nREPL, and ran a full verified completion — 2 branches, 20 turns, 6 confirmed artifacts across Z3 and Prolog, shipping x=9 y=4 for 3x+5y=47 with x>y. So the binary is no longer limited to engine paths and a local plain-http provider.

nREPL now starts in a binary as well. That was never a separate defect: it only failed because the workaround for 9pl needed a runtime require, which jolt build cannot reach statically. Removing the workaround removed it.

The static-reachability constraint itself still stands and the CI build job still guards it.

title: Loading jolt.nrepl before any TLS handshake breaks https for the process
description:
Loading `jolt.nrepl` into a process that has not yet completed a TLS handshake leaves `jolt.http-client` unable to complete one afterwards. Every https call then throws an opaque Chez condition. Plain http keeps working.

Characterized precisely:

- A prior SUCCESSFUL https call immunizes the process. Loading nREPL after that is harmless.
- A FAILED https call does not immunize it.
- A plain-http call does not immunize it.
- Constructing an `SSL_CTX` by hand through `jolt.http.tls` does not immunize it.

So it is initialization order, not ongoing interference, and whatever gets initialized sits deeper than context creation.

The workaround is in `veriframe.core`: warm the TLS path against the configured provider, then load and start nREPL. It doubles as the boot-time key validation the TypeScript harness also does, so it is not pure overhead. `veriframe.smoke/nrepl-load-order-check` spawns a subprocess in the real startup order and fails if the order regresses.

The cost is that the workaround needs a runtime `require`, which an AOT binary cannot resolve. See veriframe-clj-sqf: nREPL simply does not start in a built binary.

Worth reporting upstream against jolt-lang/jolt with the four-way characterization above, since that is most of the diagnostic work.
close_reason:
Fixed upstream in jolt-lang/http-client cc45d7e, and the four-way characterization in this bead turned out to be the tell. Chez resolves a foreign symbol against loaded shared objects most-recent-first, and defcfn resolves when the def is evaluated, so whichever object loaded last before jolt.http.tls decides who owns SSL_*. On macOS the process image transitively links /usr/lib/libssl.dylib, which is LibreSSL. jolt.nrepl calls (ffi/load-library) with no argument at ns load to bind sockets, which loads the process's own symbols and therefore puts LibreSSL ahead of the OpenSSL that :jolt/native loaded.

The failure was not a missing symbol but a silent mix: TLS_client_method from one implementation and SSL_CTX_new from the other, whose SSL_CTX layouts disagree, so the first call through it died with 'invalid memory reference'. OpenSSL_version confirmed it directly — OpenSSL 3.6.2 without the nrepl require, LibreSSL 3.3.6 with it.

That also explains why a prior SUCCESSFUL https call immunized the process and a hand-built SSL_CTX did not: what mattered was whether the tls bindings had already resolved, not any ongoing state.

jolt.http.tls now loads libcrypto and then libssl itself immediately before its bindings resolve, so load order no longer decides. veriframe.core drops the workaround: jolt.nrepl is a plain static require in the ns form again, which is also what gets nREPL into a built binary. smoke/nrepl-load-order-check still passes.

title: Share one Mathlib environment across branches instead of a session each
description:
Every branch builds its own Lean session and pays `import Mathlib` in full. Measured: 377927ms, and a second import in the same process is no cheaper (384334ms then 375026ms), so the cost is CPU-bound elaboration rather than disk and nothing amortises it. A warmed session is 0.83GB RSS.

So a beam of 5 that uses Lean wants 5 warmed sessions: about 4.2GB and 5 imports at startup, parallelisable but competing for the same cores. veriframe-clj-j3j made this survivable by warming at boot, and left the scaling alone.

The structural fix is that branches do not each need their own PROCESS, only their own ENVIRONMENT. The repl protocol is already environment-addressed: `run-command` takes an `env` id and `mathlib-env` is just the id `import Mathlib` produced. One session could hold the Mathlib env and hand every branch a distinct child env, at one import and one 0.83GB heap for the whole beam.

What makes it real work is that send-command serialises on a compare-and-set busy flag and KILLS a session that is asked for something while busy, which is correct for the current one-session-per-branch design and fatal for a shared one: any two branches calling Lean in the same round would kill the session for everyone. Sharing needs a request queue with per-branch fairness, and the abandoned-turn problem that motivated kill-on-busy has to be solved some other way — probably by tracking which branch owns an in-flight request and discarding its reply rather than killing the process.

Also needs care on isolation. The current model gives each branch a whole process, so a branch that defines a broken instance or leaves a `sorry` in scope cannot affect another. Child environments are weaker than that and the boundary would want a test that one branch's declarations are invisible to another.

Worth doing only if Lean turns out to be used often enough to matter. The cheap alternative is to keep one session per branch and set HARNESS_LEAN_WARM_SESSIONS to the beam width, paying memory for simplicity.
notes: See the correction on veriframe-clj-j3j. The per-branch import cost that motivates this is largely a memory-pressure artifact of the dev machine: the same import is ~10s on CI where the oleans stay in page cache. The memory argument survives (0.83GB per warmed session), the latency argument mostly does not. Re-measure on the target machine before taking this on.

title: A slow-trickle provider still cannot be bounded by the turn deadline
description:
SO_RCVTIMEO bounds INACTIVITY, not total call duration. jolt.http.tls now applies the caller's :socket-timeout to the socket under OpenSSL (fixed in http-client cc45d7e), which closes the observed failure: a peer that accepts the connection and then goes silent. It does not close the general case.

A provider that trickles a byte every few seconds resets the per-recv timer forever, so the call never times out and the scheduler's per-turn deadline (default 420s) is still unenforceable. A timed deref cannot preempt a thread inside a blocking foreign call, so the only bound available is the one the socket enforces.

Not observed in practice. Filed because veriframe-clj-6v9 was closed on the silent-peer case and the general claim it made should not be assumed fixed with it.

Options if it ever bites: a total-deadline watchdog that closes the fd underneath the parked reader, turning the block into the I/O error the existing catch already handles. That needs the socket handle, which jolt.http.platform does not currently hand back to a caller.

title: Embed SWI-Prolog via FFI
description:
Embed SWI-Prolog in-process via jolt.ffi, replacing the swipl subprocess.

Surface confirmed present: `SWI-Prolog.h`, `libswipl.dylib`, 1161 unmangled `PL_*`
symbols. Simplified BSD, so no licensing consequence.

## This one has the weakest case of the four

The marshalling argument that motivates the epic barely applies here. The current
implementation puts a read-eval-print server written in Prolog INSIDE swipl
(`resources/prolog/session.pl`), and it uses `library(http/json)` to return
answers as structured JSON with bindings as a map. There is no text parsing to
eliminate — the engine already hands back structure, because the harness gets to
run its own code inside it.

What FFI would add is avoiding the JSON hop and getting term handles directly,
which matters for large answer sets and not much otherwise.

## What it costs

**Threading.** The beam wants one engine per branch on separate threads. That
means `PL_create_engine` per branch and `PL_set_engine` on entry, which is the
documented multi-engine path but is a real place to get threading wrong, and this
project has already produced one FFI concurrency crash.

**Isolation.** This is the engine that loses the most. Today each branch's Prolog
is its own OS process: a runaway `label/1` over a badly-constrained CLP(FD) model
burns one process that `proc/run` can kill. In-process it burns a thread in the
shared address space that nothing can interrupt, and a crash takes every branch.
Model-written Prolog is exactly where runaway search comes from.

**The bootstrap design goes away.** `session.pl` is load-bearing in a way worth
preserving: it consults `library(clpfd)` before any harness term reaches the
reader, which is mandatory because `#>` and `#<` are operators clpfd defines at
load. In-process, the equivalent ordering has to be reconstructed against the C
API, and getting it wrong means clpfd goals fail to parse with a confusing error.

## Recommendation

Do Z3 first and reassess. If the Z3 adapter proves the shape and P0 is closed,
this becomes mechanical. If either is shaky, the honest answer for swipl may be
to leave it as a subprocess: it is the one engine where the current design
already achieves what the epic is for.

## Acceptance

- an engine per branch, created and set per thread, with a test running the beam
  width at 5 and asserting no cross-branch state leakage
- clpfd operators parse, verified by the same `X #> 2, X #< 6, label([X])` probe
  the smoke check already uses
- a runaway goal is bounded, or this does not ship — that is P0's mechanism
  applied here
- the subprocess path stays selectable and both paths agree on the registry

title: Research: whether any engine should move from subprocess to FFI
description:
Standardize on jolt.ffi for every engine, replacing subprocess-and-pipes.

## Decision and rationale

The reason is marshalling, not latency. Against a 30-second provider call the
difference between a 5ms in-process call and a 300ms subprocess round-trip is
noise, and any argument resting on speed here is a weak one. What in-process buys
is structured values: a live handle returns objects that can be read as objects,
where a subprocess returns printed text that has to be parsed.

engine/smt.clj is the standing evidence. parse-model is a hand-rolled
paren-balancing walk over Z3's printed `(get-model)` output, it already needed a
special case for negatives printed as `(- 5)`, and it is the most fragile code in
the engines — because printed text is all a subprocess gives back.

The secondary gain is genuine incremental state. Z3_solver_push/pop, a persistent
Prolog engine, a live Octave workspace: a branch builds a problem up across turns
and pops a bad hypothesis, rather than re-submitting the whole encoding every
turn the way verify_smt does today.

## Gated on veriframe-clj-6v9, and this is not a formality

Expressed as a blocks edge on veriframe-clj-479, the reference implementation,
because beads will not let an epic be blocked by a task. That is the right place
for it regardless: the bindings can be written and tested against P0 unfixed,
but no FFI engine becomes the DEFAULT until an engine call can be bounded.

The two components already using jolt.ffi produced the two worst bugs in this
project:

- jolt-lang/db: concurrent sqlite3_prepare_v2 on one connection handle gave
  `invalid memory reference` and failed all fourteen benchmark problems.
- jolt-lang/http-client: a socket read that no timeout can preempt. That is P0,
  the bug that killed the benchmark sweep and froze a beam for fifteen minutes.

P0 is precisely an unbounded blocking FFI call inside a branch thread. Every
engine converted to FFI turns an engine call into that same shape. Today a hung
swipl is bounded because proc/run kills the process tree; a hung
PL_next_solution is not killable and not interruptible, and a timed deref will
not preempt it.

So this epic, done before P0, makes the harness strictly MORE fragile: it removes
the process boundary that currently contains an engine hang and replaces it with
the exact failure mode we already cannot handle. P0 first.

## What is also given up

Isolation. Today each branch gets its own OS process per engine, so a runaway or
a crash is contained to one branch. In-process, every branch's engine state
shares one address space and one heap: a segfault in any of them takes the run
and every other branch with it. The input is model-generated and adversarial by
nature — the SMT and Prolog linters exist because models emit encodings that are
wrong in surprising ways — so this is the case where isolation was earning its
keep.

Compensating for that is part of the epic, not a follow-up:

- an installed error handler per engine, so a bad input is an error rather than
  an abort. Z3_set_error_handler is the model; each engine needs its equivalent
  identified.
- explicit lifetime discipline. Z3 refcounts with inc_ref/dec_ref, swipl has
  engines and frames, Octave has its own. A leak per verify_* call across a long
  beam is not hypothetical.
- every subprocess path retained behind a config flag, subprocess remaining the
  default per engine until that engine's FFI path has run a full benchmark sweep
  without a crash. Two paths disagreeing on one input is also how a binding bug
  gets caught, which no single-path test can do.

## The standard shape

For this to be a standard rather than four separate ports, every engine adapter
gets the same surface, matching what engine/prolog.clj and engine/lean_repl.clj
already expose so nothing above them changes:

    create-session   -> a handle, per branch
    alive?           -> bool
    dispose!         -> best effort, never throws past the caller
    <engine ops>     -> {:ok bool ...}, never raw values or exceptions

Plus, carried over from the subprocess sessions because both were needed in
practice:

- a compare-and-set busy flag, and a session killed rather than waited on when a
  previous request was abandoned. This came out of an abandoned turn wedging its
  session monitor forever.
- a structured marshalling layer with round-trip tests of its own. This is the
  justification for the whole epic, so it is tested directly rather than
  incidentally through a tool.

## Children, ordered by difficulty

Z3 (veriframe-clj-479) is first and is the reference implementation: 789
unmangled Z3_* symbols in z3_api.h, MIT, no shim, no build step. Whatever shape
it lands in becomes the standard the others follow.

SWI-Prolog is second: SWI-Prolog.h, libswipl.dylib, 1161 PL_* symbols,
Simplified BSD. Pure C, but embedding a Prolog VM brings its own threading
rules — PL_create_engine and PL_set_engine per branch thread, since the beam
wants an engine per branch on separate threads. It also loses the most from
isolation, because the current bootstrap-server design is genuinely good and
already returns structured JSON.

Lean is third and may not be worth doing. lean/lean.h and libleanshared exist
and Lean is Apache-2.0, but leanprover-community/repl is a Lean PROGRAM, so
converting means reimplementing its elaboration and tactic-state handling against
the C API. Embedding the elaborator with Mathlib imported is not a documented
path. The repl already speaks structured JSON, so the marshalling argument that
motivates this epic barely applies. Investigate before committing.

Octave (veriframe-clj-15u) is last on effort though it prompted the epic: C++
only, so it needs an extern "C" shim and a C++ toolchain, and it is why the
project relicensed to GPLv3.

## Where to stop

Two things stay as they are. The provider HTTP client is already FFI and is the
source of P0; it does not need more FFI, it needs its blocking call bounded. And
nothing here argues for converting SQLite further — jolt-lang/db is already FFI
and the lesson from it was to serialize access, not to go deeper.

## Acceptance for the epic

- one adapter shape, shared by every converted engine, with the marshalling
  layer tested by round-trip rather than through a tool
- P0 closed, or a bounded-call mechanism landed that each FFI engine uses
- every engine's subprocess path still selectable, and a test that both paths
  agree on the benchmark registry
- a full benchmark sweep completes with all converted engines in FFI mode
- resident memory flat across a thousand calls per engine
notes:
Further evidence against, from the licence work on 2026-08-05. The Octave engine was the one case with a clear FFI motivation, and it moves to a subprocess: in-process linking would make the combined work GPLv3, which veriframe cannot be, because jolt is EPL-2.0 without the secondary-licence option and three more dependencies are EPL-1.0 by inheritance from Clojure code. The FSF lists EPL as GPL-incompatible.

So the licence now constrains this question and not just the engineering. Any GPL-licensed engine is off the table in-process and fine as a subprocess. Z3 (MIT) and SWI-Prolog (BSD) are unaffected and remain the only candidates where FFI is a free choice.

title: Add GNU Octave as a numerical engine, as a subprocess
description:
Add GNU Octave as a fourth engine, alongside SWI-Prolog, Z3 and Lean.

## What it buys

The three current engines cover relational and finite-domain search, decidable
theories, and formal proof. None of them does numerical linear algebra, ODEs,
optimisation over reals, or signal processing. A model asked whether a matrix is
positive definite, what the condition number of a system is, or whether an
iteration converges currently has nothing to put the question through.

## Decided: in-process, as a REPL

The project relicensed to GPLv3 to take this route, so the linking question is
settled and the subprocess alternative below is recorded only as the road not
taken.

Octave is embedded as a live interpreter with persistent workspace state, in the
same shape as the Prolog and Lean sessions: a session per branch, commands
evaluated against accumulated state, so a branch can build a problem up across
turns instead of resubmitting it whole.

The reason for in-process is NOT latency. Against a 30-second provider call the
difference between a 5ms in-process call and a 300ms subprocess round-trip is
noise, and an earlier version of this bead recommended the subprocess on exactly
that weak argument. The real reason is MARSHALLING: a live interpreter hands back
octave_value objects that can be read structurally, where a subprocess hands back
printed text that has to be parsed. engine/smt.clj shows what that costs —
parse-model is a hand-rolled paren-balancer over Z3's printed output because text
is all it gets, and it is the most fragile code in the engines. A numerical engine
returning matrices makes that worse, not better: shapes, types, complex values and
NaN all have to survive the round trip, and printed output loses or mangles each
of them.

Note the contrast with veriframe-clj-479, which does the same thing for Z3: Z3
exports a stable unmangled C API and is MIT, so it needs no shim and no
relicense. Octave is the harder of the two on both counts, which is why it is
lower priority despite being the one that prompted the license change.

## What the C++ API actually requires

Octave's official API is C++: `octave::interpreter` from `octave/interpreter.h`,
with `octave::feval` for calls, in `liboctave` / `liboctinterp`.

jolt.ffi binds C symbols. C++ methods are name-mangled and the mangling is not
stable across compilers or Octave releases, so `ffi/defcfn` cannot bind
`octave::interpreter::execute()` directly. The FFI route therefore needs a thin
`extern "C"` shim compiled against the Octave headers and shipped as a shared
library, with jolt.ffi binding the shim rather than Octave. That is the standard
pattern and it is a real build step: the shim needs mkoctfile or a C++ toolchain
plus Octave's dev headers on every machine that builds it, which the other three
engines do not.

## Licensing: settled

Done. The project is GPLv3 as of the commit that files this, changed from
Apache-2.0 specifically so liboctave can be linked. Apache-2.0 is one-way
compatible with GPLv3, so the earlier history carries forward.

Worth knowing that the three engines shipping today are all separate processes
and needed no such change; this is the first thing that does.

## The road not taken

A long-lived `octave-cli` subprocess over stdin would have needed no shim, no C++
toolchain and no relicense, and would have reused the two existing session
wrappers including the busy-flag guard from the abandoned-turn fix. It was
rejected because it cannot return structured values, only printed text.

If the shim turns out to be a maintenance problem, this is the fallback, and the
cost of switching is the marshalling layer plus accepting text parsing.

## The harder problem: what does a numerical result verify?

This is the part that needs design work rather than plumbing, and it is why this
should not be wired up as "another verify_* tool" without thought.

Every existing engine returns a discrete verdict. Prolog succeeds or fails, Z3
says sat or unsat, Lean elaborates or does not. Octave returns a float. A float
is not a proof, and the done gate rests entirely on the artifact classification
being trustworthy.

Concretely:

- `claim_status` is confirmed / refuted / ambiguous / existential. A numerical
  result is none of those. "Confirmed to within 1e-9" is not confirmed, and
  recording it as such would launder approximations into the one field the done
  gate trusts. It probably needs a fifth bucket, or a tolerance recorded
  alongside the verdict so the auditor can see what was actually established.
- The verification has to be a residual or a bound, not an equality. Checking
  `A*x == b` in floating point is meaningless; checking `norm(A*x - b) < tol`
  with `tol` declared up front by the model is the analogue of the
  `expectedVerdict` argument verify_smt already requires.
- `tools/uncovered-tokens` compares answer tokens against artifact text. An
  answer saying 3.14159 against an artifact holding 3.141592653589793 will not
  match, so the claim-evidence gate needs numeric-aware comparison or it will
  block every correct numerical answer.
- Octave will happily return `NaN`, `Inf` or a silently truncated result. Those
  are the numerical equivalent of the vacuous-encoding failures the SMT linter
  exists to catch, and they need the same treatment: refuse rather than report.

## Integration points in this codebase

- `native/octave_shim.cc` plus a build step, and its own CI job
- `engine/octave.clj`, session-shaped like `engine/prolog.clj`, holding an
  interpreter handle rather than a process handle
- a marshalling layer both ways: Clojure values to octave_value and back,
  covering real and complex scalars, matrices with their shape, strings, bools,
  and the empty matrix. This is the part that justifies the whole approach, so
  it gets tests of its own rather than being incidental to the tool
- a lint pass in `engine/lint.clj` for the vacuous cases above
- `verify_octave` in `agent/tools.clj`, requiring a declared tolerance
- `:octave` under `:engines` in `config.clj`, and in the `/health` engine report
- `bench/problems.clj` entries, including a probe that a numerical near-miss is
  NOT recorded as confirmed
- the `fast` and `smoke` CI jobs install it; `apt-get install octave` on the
  runner

## Acceptance

- values round-trip through the marshalling layer without losing shape, type or
  precision, including complex values and the empty matrix, and a round-trip
  test is what proves the in-process choice earned its cost
- an interpreter that dies is detected and the session marked dead rather than
  wedging, the same guard the Prolog and Lean sessions carry
- a claim verified within a declared tolerance is recorded with that tolerance
  visible, and a claim outside it is refuted
- NaN, Inf and dimension-mismatch results are refused by the lint, not reported
- a probe problem confirms that a numerically-close-but-wrong answer does not
  ship, mutation-tested by loosening the tolerance check and watching it fail
- the licensing decision is written down in the README, whichever way it goes
notes:
APPROACH CHANGED on 2026-08-05: subprocess, not in-process FFI.

This bead was written around embedding Octave's C++ interpreter through a C shim, and the licence consequence was accepted deliberately: Octave is GPLv3, linking it makes the combined work GPLv3, and veriframe was relicensed from Apache-2.0 to GPLv3 ahead of the work.

That relicence turns out not to be possible. Checking what the dependencies are actually licensed under:

    jolt (runtime + stdlib)     EPL-2.0, secondary-licence option NOT exercised
    clojure/data.json           EPL-1.0
    clojure/tools.logging       EPL-1.0
    jolt-lang/logging           EPL-1.0 (port of tools.logging)

The FSF lists EPL as GPL-incompatible in both versions; EPL-2.0 is compatible only where the secondary-licence option is declared, and jolt's Exhibit A is the unfilled template, which its own text says is not sufficient. Three of those four are EPL by inheritance from Clojure code and are not ours to relicense at all. So a GPLv3 veriframe cannot legally link the platform it runs on, and in-process Octave was the only thing requiring GPLv3.

veriframe is EPL-2.0 as of this change, and Octave becomes a subprocess like z3 and swipl. The FSF's own position is that separate programs communicating over pipes are not a combined work, so Octave's GPL does not reach across the boundary and no relicence is needed.

What this costs, honestly. The marshalling argument that the in-process design rested on was already the weaker one after `jsonencode` came up: a subprocess CAN return structured output the way the Prolog session does. JSON still loses complex values, distinguishes poorly between a 1x1 matrix and a scalar, and round-trips floats through decimal text, so an engine that needs exact numerics will feel it. Worth measuring against a real problem before deciding the fidelity is inadequate.

What it buys, beyond the licence. The same isolation the other engines have: a runaway or crashing Octave takes one branch rather than the run, which matters because the input is model-generated and adversarial. And it can be killed unconditionally through engine/proc.clj, which an in-process call cannot be.

Implementation now looks like the Prolog engine rather than a new pattern: a long-lived `octave --no-gui --quiet` session speaking line-framed JSON via `jsonencode`, with resources/octave/session.m playing the part resources/prolog/session.pl plays. See veriframe-clj-5dn for whether any engine should move to FFI, which this is now evidence against.

title: Investigate embedding Lean via FFI, and probably decline
description:
Investigate whether embedding Lean via FFI is worth doing. Likely answer: no.

Surface exists — `lean/lean.h` and `libleanshared_1.dylib` / `libleanshared_2.dylib`
in the toolchain, Apache-2.0 licensed — so this is not blocked on availability.

## Why it is probably not worth it

`leanprover-community/repl` is a Lean PROGRAM, not a library with a C entry
point. Converting does not mean binding a few symbols; it means reimplementing
its elaboration, environment handling and tactic-state machinery against the C
API. Embedding the elaborator with Mathlib imported is not a documented path, and
`lean.h` is aimed at calling C from Lean and at embedding the runtime, not at
driving the frontend.

And the epic's own justification does not apply. The repl already speaks
structured JSON over pipes; there is no printed output being parsed. What FFI
would remove is a pipe and a JSON encode, against reimplementing the hardest
frontend of the four engines.

## What it would cost that the others do not

Mathlib in-process. The import currently costs tens of seconds per session and
sits in a separate address space where its memory is reclaimed on dispose. In
process, that footprint joins the harness's own, multiplied by branches, and a
beam of five would hold five Mathlib environments in one heap.

## Scope of this task

Investigation, not implementation. Answer three questions and write the answer
into this bead:

- can the elaborator be driven through `lean.h` with Mathlib imported, or does
  it require running Lean-side code
- what is the in-process memory cost of one Mathlib environment, and does it
  multiply per branch or share
- is there an upstream C entry point planned, which would make this cheap later

Close as "not doing" with the reasoning recorded if the answers are what they
look like. That is a useful outcome and cheaper than finding out during
implementation.
